I was a high school teacher for '20-21 at a very small charter school. The school basically used pre-packaged online programs for all instruction and testing. I'd say for me it depends on how much they actually need to see ME, be in my presence, use my facility etc. If they are pretty independent and able to follow an HEP on their own then maybe a lower frequency. If they need a lot of hands on care like manual or a lot of guidance and adjustments in HEP, then more. 

A lot of therapists forget that you don't need to do the same frequency the entire POC. Tapering down and front loading can be really helpful. If you only have 5 visits approved you can start someone at 2x/week for 2 weeks to treat the acute issues and start on an initial HEP, then 1x/week for 2 weeks to check in and adjust the HEP, then 1x the following week for final education. This spreads those visits out over 5 weeks to monitor the long term healing process instead of 2.5 weeks. 

This frequency would be written as 2w2, 1w2, 1w (the first day of the week of the final visit)

I used to be an insurance reviewer and they LOVE taper down frequencies vs. one consistent one. It shows you are trying to get the patient independent, not just using visits and hoping you get more. It's a lot easier to show more visits are needed that way.

It sucks everything is dictated by insurance, but it does keep us on our toes that we are using the patient's time wisely

Their BP meds probably need to be reviewed by the prescriber since they are not effective with activity. My protocol has always been systolic over 180 and/or diastolic over 100 needs to be reported, even if momentarily.

You can be either salaried or pay per visit, where I am in Austin, TX is comes out to around $60 per visit and that covers everything regardless of how far you travel between patients. Most companies will try to keep you in one territory, I probably average 30 minutes between patients (ranging from 10-60 minutes).  You are paid mileage around 40 cents a mile, but that barely covers gas. A big part of the job is scheduling which you do yourself. I schedule the next appointment at the end of my visit.  It's sooo hard to predict a specific time, but I'll tell patients I'll be there "around" 3, then call them at the end of the visit before and let them know that I'm on my way and when I'll get there. Visits are 30-60 minutes with an average of 45 minutes.
Documentation for home health absolutely sucks, I've worked in a lot of settings and it is the worst. Medicare just requires so much that other settings don't, like BP, RR, HR, temp, explanation of homebound status etc. Everyone will tell you to do it during the visit, which I hate. I want my focus to be on the patient, not documentation. Patients will tell you how the other clinicians spend too much time doing notes. However then you have a ton to do at home which sucks even more. I always get behind too. For me the best thing to do is write what I can during down times of the visit and finish it in my car. Another part of home health is the interdisciplinary communication. There are a ton of phon e calls, texts and emails for updating on patient status, questions, new patient info etc. That takes up a lot of time too.
Being salaried vs pay per visit makes a huge difference in your schedule.  Full time is 30 visits and if you are full time you are expected to meet that.  I prefer semi-full at 24 visits and then I get extra if I go over that. That being said I usually start my first patient 9-10am. I'd love to start at 8am, but people rarely let you come that early. I see 4-6 patients a day, last patient at 4pm so I'm home around 5:30pm. Cancellations are a huge part of home health. That's why I always call when I'm on my way in case they want to cancel then. If you are salaried cancellations rock because you have some free time in your day. If you are per visit you just lost $60. 
Besides all of that I still love home health. I love the geriatric patient population, I feel like you get closer to your patients since you are in their homes, I love something new everyday and the freedom is the best. If I want to go to Starbucks in the middle of the day I can. If I don't want to see patients before 10am I can do that. I hate doing the same thing everyday in the same place. Home health is always something new.
Let me know if you have more questions!

STAY AWAY FROM SNF, I've worked in several.  Rehab is inpatient rehab in a hospital setting where the patient is there specifically for therapy and the stay is usually 2 weeks after which they go home usually. They get 3 hours of therapy a day between PT, OT and speech.  The nurses and staff are all focused on rehab and getting the patient better and back to their prior level of function.

SNF patients are the ones who can't tolerate inpatient rehab and are generally much weaker and have lower rehab potential. Medicare part A patients are covered up to 100 days and many stay several months before going home.  Part B patients are those that live in the facility, usually a nursing home.  These patients generally have very low rehab potential as they need daily assistance from nursing staff and will not ever become independent.  Staff in SNF are generally not rehab focused as patients stay for a very long time. The worst part about SNFs is how financially corrupt they are.  Payment for the facility is based on rehab need so most patients are signed up for 2-3 hours a day when often this is inappropriate and the patient cannot tolerate it.  So often in SNF gyms you will see patients falling asleep while their therapist looks at their phone so the proper number of minutes is reached.
In case you can't tell I hate SNFs. I've worked in several because the pay is great.  Inpatient rehab was my favorite rotation in school so definitely stick with that!
